title: My Clinic — Facility Management & Safety
description: New-staff course on the eight CBAHI Facility Management & Safety plans, MOH emergency codes and ISO 45001 rights.

metadata.description: New-staff course on the eight CBAHI Facility Management & Safety plans, MOH emergency codes and ISO 45001 rights.

objectives.description: Name the eight FMS plans and match each to its purpose.
Apply the AREC cycle and the hierarchy of controls to a workplace hazard.
Match each MOH emergency code to its meaning and follow the common response pattern.
Respond to a fire using RACE and PASS, choosing the correct extinguisher and evacuation type.
Interpret GHS pictograms and the NFPA diamond, decide on Code Orange, and segregate waste correctly.
Apply ID, visitor, contractor and premises security rules.
Identify emergency power, utility shut-offs and HVAC rules in a clinical area.
Take faulty or overdue medical equipment out of use and report it to Biomedical Engineering.
Apply ALARA, dose-limit bands and laser classes to stay safe near radiation and lasers.
Combine the plans in one connected emergency (capstone).

screens.title: First-week safety challenge
screens.body_html:
Can you keep your clinic safe in your first week?

9 missions: 1 The eight FMS plans · 2 Occupational Health & Safety · 3 Emergency codes · 4 Fire safety · 5 Hazardous materials & waste · 6 Security · 7 Utilities · 8 Medical equipment · 9 Radiation & laser

Earn XP: +10 for each activity you get right · +5 for each quick check · +2 for each screen you explore. Ranks: Newcomer → Safety Spotter → Safety Ally → Safety Champion.

XP is just for you: it never counts towards your pass mark.
screens.notes: Gamification (tools/gamify.py, decision D18).
screens.media_alt: Illustration for the first-week safety challenge.

screens.title: Why the FMS chapter exists
screens.body_html:
• Survey requirement — surveyors check all eight plans: documents, staff knowledge, physical evidence.
  • Everyone's responsibility — every employee knows their role.
  • One connected system — plans and emergency codes overlap.

CBAHI chapter wording ⚠ Draft — pending 01/B9
screens.narration_text: Noor: The chapter is a survey requirement, a shared responsibility, and one connected system. Notice which part of the information you would need first in practice. Use that as the starting point for a safe, respectful next action. Carry the idea into your next decision. Notice which part of this you would use first on shift. The aim is a decision you can repeat, not a phrase to recall. Link it to the task waiting for you tomorrow.

screens.title: Explore the eight plans
screens.prompt_html: Open all eight plans. Each one protects against a different physical risk.
screens.image_alt: Eight Facility Management and Safety plans shown as icons.

regions.feedback_html:
Purpose: Protect people from harm caused by fire and smoke.

Main functions: Prevention and routine inspections · Detection and suppression systems · Code Red response (RACE/PASS) · Evacuation routes and drills

Purpose: Keep the physical environment free of hazards.

Main functions: Environmental and safety rounds · Hazard identification and correction · Construction/renovation risk assessment · Safety signage and wayfinding

Purpose: Safely manage chemicals and medical waste end to end.

Main functions: Inventory, SDS and GHS/NFPA labelling · Safe storage, handling and transport · Code Orange spill response · Waste segregation and disposal

Purpose: Keep essential utility systems running safely.

Main functions: Critical system inventory · Preventive maintenance · Backup power and water continuity · Code Brown response

Purpose: Make sure medical equipment is safe and working.

Main functions: Equipment inventory and inspection · Planned preventive maintenance (PPM) · Incident and recall management · User training

Purpose: Protect people, property and information.

Main functions: Access control and ID badges · Visitor and contractor management · CCTV monitoring · Response to Codes White, Silver, Black and Pink

Purpose: Prepare for emergencies that start inside the facility.

Main functions: Emergency code activation · Emergency Response Team (ERT) roles · Continuity of critical services · Regular internal drills

Purpose: Prepare for mass-casualty or community events.

Main functions: Surge capacity planning · Coordination with Civil Defence, MOH and Red Crescent · Code Yellow triage and communication · Community drills

A fire is a Code Red. A chemical spill is a Code Orange.

screens.title: Match the plans
screens.prompt_html: Match each plan to its purpose.

pairs.right_html: Protect people from harm caused by fire and smoke.
Keep the physical environment free of hazards.
Safely manage chemicals and medical waste end to end.
Keep essential utility systems running safely.
Make sure medical equipment is safe and working.
Prepare for emergencies that start inside the facility.
Prepare for mass-casualty or community events.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Each plan covers one physical risk; together they protect patients, staff and visitors.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Look for the risk each plan protects against: fire and smoke, the building, chemicals and waste, utilities, equipment, people and property, inside events or community events. The correct set is shown below.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: Four core terms
screens.prompt_html: Flip each card: term on the front, meaning and an example on the back.

cards.back_html: Complete physical, mental and social well-being — not only the absence of injury or illness.
Freedom from conditions that cause injury, illness or damage, achieved by controlling hazards before they cause harm.
Anything that could cause harm. Example: a wet floor, an unlabelled chemical, an exposed wire.
How likely the hazard is to cause harm, combined with how severe that harm would be. Example: a wet floor near a busy waiting area.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Risk is likelihood plus severity. A hazard is the thing, risk is the chance it hurts someone. Reveal each card, then pause to recall the point before moving on. Link the term with the action it should prompt in practice. If one detail stays with you, let it be the safe one. Ask early when a situation does not match the rule.

screens.title: Incident types
screens.prompt_html: Open each incident type.

items.title: Near miss — most valuable to report
items.body_html: Nothing happened, but it easily could have. Reporting it is free learning.

items.title: First aid case
items.body_html: Minor injury treated with on-site first aid; no further medical care.

items.title: Medical treatment case
items.body_html: Needs treatment beyond first aid, such as stitches or prescribed medication.

items.title: Lost time injury
items.body_html: The employee cannot return to normal duties for a period.

items.title: Fatality
items.body_html: Death from a workplace incident; triggers mandatory investigation and regulatory reporting.

screens.narration_text: Noor: A near miss is the most valuable report: it is free learning. Use each section to build the picture step by step. Before moving on, identify the action or check that belongs to your role. Ask early when a situation does not match the rule. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear.

screens.title: The AREC cycle
screens.prompt_html: AREC is a habit before every task. Hazard awareness is never a one-time task.
screens.image_alt: AREC cycle: Anticipate, Recognise, Evaluate, Control.

labels.text: Anticipate — think ahead before the task
Recognise — spot hazards as they appear
Control — use the hierarchy, top first

feedback.correct_html: Anticipate, recognise, evaluate, control — then start again. Use it before every task.
feedback.incorrect_html: Read each stage: the cycle repeats because hazards change.

screens.narration_text: Noor: AREC as a habit before every task, not a form. Read each label as a prompt for what to check or who should act next. The useful step is linking the visual with a real decision. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check.

screens.title: Hierarchy of controls
screens.prompt_html: Put the controls in order, from most to least effective.

items.text_html: Engineering controls — isolate people from the hazard

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Start at the top: the higher a control sits, the more reliably it removes the risk. PPE is the last line of defence, not the first.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Removing or replacing the hazard protects everyone; PPE only protects the person wearing it. PPE is the last line of defence, not the first.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose. Use the rule you practised.

screens.title: The trailing cable
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-neutral}}Noor · Safety liaison

A power cable trails across the walkway beside the patient waiting area. Patients and visitors are walking past.

nodes.prompt_html: You spot the cable. What do you do first?

choices.text_html: Stop, warn people nearby and keep them clear while you assess the risk.
choices.feedback_html: Best choice. You recognised the hazard and protected people first. Now evaluate it and choose a control.

choices.text_html: Step over it and carry on; someone else will report it.
choices.feedback_html: Not safe. A trip hazard beside patients is everyone's responsibility. Recognising it and doing nothing leaves the risk in place.

choices.text_html: Go and complete an incident form before doing anything else.
choices.feedback_html: Reporting matters, but not before people are protected. Someone could trip while you are away.

choices.text_html: Re-route the cable away from the walkway.
choices.feedback_html: Strongest. Removing the hazard from the walkway sits at the top of the hierarchy — nobody can trip on it.

choices.text_html: Cover the cable with a cable protector.
choices.feedback_html: Better than a sign, but the cable is still in the walkway. Removing it from the path is stronger.

choices.text_html: Put up a warning sign.
choices.feedback_html: A sign is an administrative control. It relies on people noticing it, so it is weaker than removing the hazard.

choices.text_html: Warn each person who walks past.
choices.feedback_html: Warning people is the weakest option here. It depends on you being there every time.

nodes.prompt_html: Your supervisor says: “Leave it, we're busy.” What do you do?

choices.text_html: Use your right to stop unsafe work and contact your Department Safety Liaison.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. Under ISO 45001 you can stop work you believe could cause serious harm, without fear of retaliation. Your Safety Liaison is the bridge to EHS.

choices.text_html: Leave it; the supervisor has decided.
choices.feedback_html: The hazard is still there. Your rights exist so that safety concerns are never silenced by fear of consequences.

choices.text_html: Ignore the supervisor and argue in front of patients.
choices.feedback_html: The concern is valid, but raise it through the right route: stop the unsafe work and contact your Safety Liaison or Safety Officer.

feedback.correct_html: You put people first, chose the strongest control and used your rights.
feedback.incorrect_html: Review AREC and the hierarchy of controls, then try again. People first; remove the hazard if you can; you may stop unsafe work.

screens.title: Who to contact and your rights
screens.prompt_html: Who to contact, and your rights under ISO 45001.

items.title: Department Safety Liaison
items.body_html: Your first contact for hazards, risk assessments and PPE questions. Don't know yours? Ask your supervisor on day 1.

items.title: Right to stop unsafe work
items.body_html: Stop any task you believe could cause serious harm, without fear of retaliation.

items.title: Right to be consulted
items.body_html: If you are afraid to stop work yourself, raise the concern with your Safety Officer or supervisor.

items.title: Right to training
items.body_html: Be trained on the hazards and safe procedures of your role before you do it.

screens.notes: Companion: Dr. Omar, char-omar-avatar-neutral + tip card, L3 bottom-left. Tip: a doctor can stop unsafe work too — “I have, and nobody blamed me.” Speaker: Dr. Omar. ISO 45001 rights wording ⚠ Draft — pending 01/B9.

Read the sections in sequence, then compare the points that matter most in practice. Keep the next action clearer than the terminology. Keep the next action clear. screens.title: Two announcements

blocks.html: Two facility-wide announcements are not colour codes:

Hospital Evacuation

Evacuate the building. Follow your unit's evacuation plan to the outdoor assembly point.

End of Disaster

The Incident Commander confirms the emergency is over. Stand down only on this signal.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Evacuation and End of Disaster are announcements, not colours. Only stand down on the official all-clear. As you read, focus on the decision this information supports in your own role. The aim is a practical next action, not a phrase to memorise. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task.

screens.title: Check: after the fire
screens.prompt_html: Quick check (not scored). The fire is out, so staff can go back to their rooms.

feedback.correct_html: Right — it's false. Stand down only when the Incident Commander gives the End of Disaster announcement.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not yet. A fire being out is not the signal. Wait for the End of Disaster announcement from the Incident Commander.

screens.title: The common response pattern
screens.prompt_html: Put the common response pattern in order. It applies to every code.

items.text_html: Recognise — notice the emergency as it develops
Activate — call switchboard/security; announce the correct code
Stand down — wait for the official all-clear

feedback.correct_html: Correct. And remember: stand down only when the official all-clear is announced.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. You must recognise it before you can activate a code, and you resume normal work only after the official all-clear.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: Who responds: the ERT
screens.prompt_html: The Emergency Response Team: five teams around an Incident Commander. You are part of the response even if you are not on it.
screens.image_alt: Emergency Response Team: Safety, Security, Nursing, Facility, Operation around an Incident Commander.

feedback.correct_html: Five teams work around one Incident Commander. Your part is to follow your role-specific response.
feedback.incorrect_html: Read each team label: the Incident Commander coordinates them all.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The ERT is five teams. You are part of the response even if you're not on it. Read each label as a prompt for what to check or who should act next. The useful step is linking the visual with a real decision.

screens.title: The fire triangle
screens.prompt_html: Remove any one side and the fire stops. Smoke, not flame, is the leading cause of death in facility fires.
screens.image_alt: Fire triangle: heat, fuel and oxygen.

feedback.correct_html: Remove heat, fuel or oxygen and the fire stops. Smoke kills first, so RACE rescues and contains before extinguishing.
feedback.incorrect_html: Read each side of the triangle: every fire control method removes one of them.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Remove one side of the triangle and the fire stops. Smoke kills first, which is why RACE rescues and contains before extinguishing. Read each label as a prompt for what to check or who should act next. The useful step is linking the visual with a real decision. Carry the idea into your next decision. Notice which part of this you would use first on shift.

screens.title: RACE: put the steps in order
screens.prompt_html: You discover a fire. Put the response in the right order.

items.text_html: Alarm — pull station + call: code, location, your ID and name
Contain — remove O₂ and alcohol rub, close doors

feedback.correct_html: Right. Smoke spreads faster than flame, so people and doors come first.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Rescue and contain come before extinguishing because smoke kills first.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: PASS: put the steps in order
screens.prompt_html: Using an extinguisher: put the PASS steps in order.

items.text_html: Aim low, at the base of the fire
Sweep side to side until it is out

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Aim at the base: that is where the fuel is burning. Use an extinguisher only on a small, contained fire.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. The pin must come out before the handle works, and you aim at the base before you squeeze and sweep.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: Find the fire safety equipment
screens.prompt_html: Open every item. Know where these are before you need them.
screens.image_alt: Clinic corridor showing a smoke detector, heat detector, sprinkler, call point, extinguisher, fire blanket, evacuation chair and assembly-point sign.

regions.feedback_html: Senses smoke early and triggers the alarm. Never cover or tamper with it.
Triggers the alarm when the temperature rises fast — used where smoke detectors would false-alarm.
Releases water automatically over a fire. Keep the space below it clear; never hang anything from it.
Manual alarm. Pull it during the Alarm step of RACE.
For a small, contained fire only. Check the class label, then use PASS.
Smothers a small fire, such as a pan or clothing fire, by cutting off oxygen.
Moves a person who cannot walk down the stairs during a vertical evacuation. Never use the elevator.
Shows the route to the outdoor assembly point used in a full evacuation. Find yours this week.
Your way out in a fire. Use the stairs, never the lift, and keep this door and the corridor clear. (Proposed — SME to confirm at review.)

screens.notes: Coordinates measured on hs1-img-corridor.png (1672×941 natural px, rect x,y,w,h). SME visual check required (asset register): confirm which ceiling device is the smoke vs heat detector (left = slotted smoke detector, right = heat detector as drawn) before release.

feedback.correct_html: You found all eight items. Look for them on your own unit this week.
feedback.incorrect_html: Open every item before you continue: you need to know where each one is before an emergency.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Walk the corridor. Know where these are before you need them. Let each marker add context rather than rushing to a conclusion. The full picture matters before a workplace decision is made. Link it to the task waiting for you tomorrow.

screens.title: Extinguisher classes
screens.prompt_html: Drag each fire to the extinguisher class that fits. Using the wrong class can make a fire worse.

targets.label_html: Class A — wood, paper, fabric, trash
Class B — flammable liquids and gases
Class K — cooking oils and fats

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Check the label before you pull the pin.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Match the fuel: ordinary materials A, liquids B, live electrical C, metals D, cooking oil K. Check the label before you pull the pin.

screens.notes: Keyboard pick-and-place is provided by the player. Full points for all correct (partial scoring not specified).
screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: Types of evacuation
screens.prompt_html: Three types of evacuation.

tabs.label: Horizontal
tabs.body_html: Move patients and staff through fire/smoke doors to the next safe compartment on the same floor. The first response for most fires.

tabs.label: Vertical
tabs.body_html: Move to a lower floor or ground level when horizontal is not enough. Use stairwells, never elevators.

tabs.label: Full
tabs.body_html: Evacuate the whole building to the outdoor assembly point. Only for the most severe, facility-wide emergencies.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Horizontal first. Vertical by stairs. Full evacuation only for the worst events. Use the tabs as a short reference, not a checklist to race through. Notice which detail would guide your next conversation or decision. Ask early when a situation does not match the rule. Good habits here are quiet: check, confirm, continue. Pause and connect this to your role. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check.

screens.title: Choose the evacuation
screens.prompt_html: Smoke is coming from Room 3. Fire doors are at the end of the corridor. Patients on the same floor are not in danger yet. What is your first move?

options.text_html: Move patients horizontally through the fire doors to the next compartment.
options.feedback_html: Correct. Horizontal evacuation is the first response for most fires: the fire doors hold back smoke.

options.text_html: Take patients down to the ground floor in the elevator.
options.feedback_html: Never use elevators in a fire. They can fail or open onto the fire floor; vertical moves use the stairwells.

options.text_html: Start a full evacuation of the building to the assembly point.
options.feedback_html: Too early. Full evacuation is for the most severe, facility-wide emergencies; moving patients beyond the fire doors is enough now.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Horizontal first; vertical by the stairs only if needed.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. The patients are not in danger yet, and fire doors are close: move them horizontally to the next compartment.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: Oxygen: myth or fact?
screens.prompt_html: True or false? Oxygen is flammable.

feedback.correct_html: Correct — it is false. Oxygen is an oxidiser. It does not burn on its own, but it makes a fire burn much faster and hotter. Keep cylinders away from flames and sparks.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Oxygen does not burn; it is an oxidiser that intensifies fire. That is why you remove oxygen cylinders when you contain a fire.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: Night shift: put RACE into action
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-neutral}}Noor · Safety liaison

Night shift. Smoke is rising from a waste bin in a patient room. The patient is in bed beside it.

choices.text_html: Move the patient away from the bin and out of the room.
choices.feedback_html: Rescue first. The patient is safe from the smoke before anything else happens.

choices.text_html: Fetch the extinguisher from the corridor.
choices.feedback_html: The patient stayed in the smoke while you were away. Smoke kills first, so rescue comes before extinguishing.

choices.text_html: Run to the nurses' station to phone switchboard.
choices.feedback_html: The alarm matters, but the patient was left beside the fire. Rescue anyone in immediate danger first.

nodes.prompt_html: You pull the call point and phone switchboard. What do you say?

choices.text_html: “Code Red, Ward 2, Room 12. My ID is 4417, my name is Sara.”
choices.feedback_html: Correct. Code type, exact location, your ID and name — the team can come straight to you.

choices.text_html: “There's a fire, come quickly!”
choices.feedback_html: Without the code and location the team loses time finding you. Always state code, location, ID and name.

choices.text_html: “Code Orange in Room 12.”
choices.feedback_html: Code Orange is a hazardous spill. A fire is Code Red; the wrong code sends the wrong team.

nodes.prompt_html: The patient is safe and the alarm is raised. How do you contain the fire?

choices.text_html: Remove the oxygen cylinder and alcohol rub, then close the door.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. Removing oxidisers and flammables and closing the door slows the smoke and fire.

choices.text_html: Open the window to let the smoke out.
choices.feedback_html: Opening a window feeds the fire with oxygen. Close doors and windows to contain it.

choices.text_html: Leave the door open so the team can find the room.
choices.feedback_html: An open door lets smoke spread down the corridor. You gave the location on the call; close the door.

nodes.prompt_html: The fire spreads past the bin. Smoke reaches the corridor. What now?

choices.text_html: Evacuate patients horizontally through the fire doors to the next compartment.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. The fire is no longer small and contained, so you evacuate. Horizontal is the first move.

choices.text_html: Keep fighting it with the extinguisher.
choices.feedback_html: An extinguisher is only for a small, contained fire. Once it grows, evacuate.

choices.text_html: Take patients down in the elevator.
choices.feedback_html: Never use elevators in a fire. Move horizontally first; use the stairwells if you must go down.

feedback.correct_html: You followed RACE under pressure: rescue, alarm, contain, then evacuate.
feedback.incorrect_html: Review RACE and the evacuation types, then try again. People and doors come first; evacuate once the fire grows.

screens.notes: Companion: Noor, char-noor-avatar-neutral (intro host) → char-noor-avatar-happy / char-noor-avatar-concern. Speaker: Noor. Ward, room, staff ID and name in node 2 are fictional training values. Avatar reaction swap per choice is not expressible; host stays neutral.

regions.feedback_html: Open flame is banned everywhere in the clinic.
Only Facilities-approved extensions; daisy-chained leads overheat.
Personal heaters and electric boilers are not allowed.
No smoking or vaping indoors.
Only approved kitchen appliances, in approved places.
Flammables stay closed, labelled and in the approved cabinet.
Hot work only with a Facilities permit.

feedback.correct_html: All seven found. Flame and fuel, unsafe electrics and blocked exits start most clinic fires. If you see one at work, remove it or report it.
feedback.incorrect_html: Keep looking: there are seven things in this room that should not be there.

Approved procurement only

No personal or unlogged purchases of hazardous substances.

feedback.correct_html: Never accept an unlabelled container.
feedback.incorrect_html: Never accept an unlabelled container: refuse it and route it through procurement.

options.text_html: Accept it and add a label yourself
options.feedback_html: A label you write is a guess. Without the supplier label and SDS, nobody knows the hazard.

options.text_html: Refuse it and send it back through procurement
options.feedback_html: Right: approved procurement only, on the inventory, with its SDS.

options.text_html: Put it in the store room until someone asks
options.feedback_html: An unknown chemical in storage is a hazard for the next person.

screens.title: GHS pictograms

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Read the pictogram before you open, mix or store a chemical, and check the SDS for details.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. The symbol shows the hazard: flame over circle is an oxidiser, the gas cylinder is pressure, the health hazard silhouette is carcinogen/toxicity. The correct set is shown below.

screens.title: Label the NFPA diamond
screens.prompt_html: Label the four areas of the NFPA 704 diamond. Each area rates a hazard from 0 (minimal) to 4 (severe).
screens.image_alt: Empty NFPA hazard diamond with four coloured quadrants.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Blue is health, red is flammability, yellow is reactivity and white holds special symbols such as W (avoid water) or OX (oxidiser).
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Use colour and the label together: blue health, red flammability, yellow reactivity, white special.

screens.title: Read a diamond
screens.prompt_html: A container's diamond shows Health 3 · Flammability 0 · Reactivity 1 · Special W. What does it tell you before opening?

options.text_html: Serious health hazard; do not use water on it.
options.feedback_html: Correct. Health 3 is a serious hazard; W in the white area means avoid water.

options.text_html: Highly flammable; keep it away from heat.
options.feedback_html: Flammability is 0: it will not burn. The high number is health.

options.text_html: Low hazard overall; handle as normal.
options.feedback_html: Health 3 is serious. Check the SDS and wear the PPE it specifies.

options.text_html: Unstable and may explode; do not move it.
options.feedback_html: Reactivity 1 is low. The main risks are health and contact with water.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Read the whole diamond: the highest number and the white area tell you the main precautions.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Higher numbers mean greater hazard. Here health is 3 and the white area says W: avoid water.

items.title: SDS at point of use

screens.title: Spill or Code Orange?
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-concern}}Noor · Safety liaison

Three spills, three decisions. Use the rule you'd follow on shift. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

nodes.prompt_html: A 200 mL bottle of alcohol hand rub falls and leaks in the corridor.

choices.text_html: Call the cleaning supervisor and warn people nearby.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. It is below the Code Orange threshold and not highly toxic. Keep people away until it is cleaned. Draft rule: 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Announce Code Orange.
choices.feedback_html: Not needed here. Code Orange is for spills at or above the threshold (draft: 500 mL), or highly toxic, reactive or explosive substances. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

nodes.prompt_html: A full 1-litre bottle of surface disinfectant splits and spreads across the treatment-room floor. (Over the draft threshold. ⚠ Draft — pending D1)

choices.text_html: Announce Code Orange.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. The spill is over the threshold, so it needs the Code Orange response. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Mop it up yourself with paper towels.
choices.feedback_html: A spill this size needs Code Orange and the right spill kit and PPE, not paper towels. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

nodes.prompt_html: A few millilitres of a highly toxic reagent spill on a lab bench.

choices.text_html: Announce Code Orange.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. Volume does not matter for a highly toxic substance: any amount is Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Call the cleaning supervisor — it is only a few mL.
choices.feedback_html: Small volume, but highly toxic. Any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance is Code Orange. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

nodes.prompt_html: Code Orange is called. Which order do you follow?

choices.text_html: Isolate and warn → PPE per SDS → contain with the right kit → report.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. Protect people first, protect yourself, then contain with the chemical or biological kit, and report to your supervisor and Safety Services.

choices.text_html: Contain with the kit → PPE per SDS → isolate and warn → report.
choices.feedback_html: Containing before isolating and protecting yourself puts you and others at risk. Isolate and warn first.

choices.text_html: Report → isolate and warn → contain → PPE per SDS.
choices.feedback_html: PPE must go on before you touch the spill, and people nearby need warning first. Report at the end.

feedback.correct_html: You applied the Code Orange rule and the four response steps. ⚠ Draft — pending D1
feedback.incorrect_html: Review the rule: 500 mL or more, or any highly toxic, reactive or explosive substance (draft). Then isolate, PPE, contain, report. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

screens.notes: Companion: Noor, char-noor-avatar-concern (intro host). Speaker: Noor. Open decision D1 (Code Orange threshold): draft uses the decision sheet's recommended value — spill ≥ 500 mL, or any highly toxic/reactive/explosive substance → Code Orange; otherwise call the cleaning supervisor. Update node 1–3 feedback and the intro when D1 closes. pass_score 3 of 4 per Phase 3 activity plan.

Infectious / biohazard — labelled biohazard bag ⚠ Draft — pending 01/B7

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Sharps go straight into the sharps container. Never recap.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Anything sharp goes in the sharps container; anything with body fluid is infectious; clean everyday trash is general. Never recap a needle.

screens.title: Security rules
screens.prompt_html: Security rules for people and premises.

tabs.label: People
tabs.body_html:
• ID always — wear your facility ID at all times.
  • Contractor permits — a valid, approved work permit before any work starts.
  • Visitor badges — visitors sign in at reception. Report anyone in a restricted area without one.

tabs.label: Premises
tabs.body_html:
• CCTV covers public areas, entrances and parking.
  • Lost and found — hand found items to Security.
  • Designated parking only.
  • No smoking anywhere, including entrances and parking.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Your badge identifies you. Everyone without one in a restricted area is your concern. Use the tabs as a short reference, not a checklist to race through. Notice which detail would guide your next conversation or decision. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.

screens.title: The visitor without a badge
screens.prompt_html: A man without a badge is in the staff-only medication room. He says he is a contractor. What is the best action?

options.text_html: Politely ask for his work permit and badge; if he has none, call Security and stay with him.
options.feedback_html: Correct. Contractors need an approved permit and ID. Calling Security without leaving him alone protects the medicines.

options.text_html: Accept his word and carry on with your work.
options.feedback_html: Risky. Anyone can say they are a contractor; without a permit and badge he should not be in a restricted area.

options.text_html: Leave the room and go to find Security.
options.feedback_html: That leaves him alone with the medicines. Call Security from where you are and stay with him.

options.text_html: Tell him to leave and say nothing more about it.
options.feedback_html: An unbadged person in a restricted area must be reported. Security needs to know, even if he leaves.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Everyone without ID in a restricted area is your concern.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Check for a permit and badge, call Security if there is none, and do not leave him alone.

screens.title: Utility walk-around
screens.prompt_html: Walk around the treatment room. Open every item.
screens.image_alt: Treatment room showing sockets, a monitor, an extension lead, a water shut-off valve and an air vent.

regions.feedback_html: Backed by generator power. Plug critical equipment in here. Generators take over within seconds of an outage. ⚠ Draft — pending 01/B6
Not backed by the generator. Know which outlets in your area are which.
The Uninterruptible Power Supply keeps critical equipment running instantly during a power cut.
A fire risk and prohibited. Remove it from use and report it; use authorised extensions only.
Know where your manual shut-off valves are, so you can act fast on a leak. Report problems to Maintenance.
Keeps air pressure and infection-control zones working. Never disable or cover isolation-room vents.

feedback.correct_html: You checked every utility point. Know which sockets are on generator power and where your shut-off valves are.
feedback.incorrect_html: Open every item before you continue: each one tells you what to do in an outage or leak.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Red sockets are on generator power. Know your shut-off valves. Isolation-room vents protect everyone. Let each marker add context rather than rushing to a conclusion. The full picture matters before a workplace decision is made. Carry the idea into your next decision. Notice which part of this you would use first on shift.

screens.title: The cold isolation room
screens.prompt_html: The isolation room is cold. A visitor asks you to close the air vent. What do you do?

options.text_html: Leave the vent open and report the temperature to Maintenance.
options.feedback_html: Correct. Isolation-room vents keep the air pressure that contains infection. Maintenance can fix the temperature safely.

options.text_html: Close the vent for a short time until the room warms up.
options.feedback_html: Even briefly, closing the vent breaks the infection-control zone. Never disable isolation-room vents.

options.text_html: Tape a cover over the vent to reduce the draught.
options.feedback_html: Covering the vent disables it. Report the problem instead.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Never disable vents in isolation rooms; report to Maintenance.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. HVAC in isolation rooms protects everyone. Keep vents open and report the problem to Maintenance.

Shows the last inspection date and status. Never use equipment past its due date.

PPM schedule

Biomedical Engineering services equipment on a fixed schedule. Report anything overdue or missing its label.

Faulty equipment is tagged and removed from use at once. Never attempt your own repair, and never relocate equipment without Biomedical Engineering.

screens.title: The overdue infusion pump
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-omar-avatar-neutral}}Dr. Omar · Family physician

A busy ward. You are about to set up an infusion pump. Its inspection label is two months overdue.

nodes.image_alt: Infusion pump with an overdue inspection label.
nodes.prompt_html: Inspection due: March. Today: May (fictional training dates). Do you use the pump?

choices.text_html: No — stop and do not use it.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. A pump past its inspection date is not known to be safe today.

choices.text_html: Yes — it seems to work, and the ward is busy.
choices.feedback_html: Working is not the same as safe. Never use equipment past its due date.

nodes.prompt_html: What do you do with the pump?

choices.text_html: Tag it “Out of Service” and remove it from use.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. The tag stops a colleague from using it by mistake.

choices.text_html: Put it back in the store room for someone else to deal with.
choices.feedback_html: Untagged, the next person may use it. Tag it out of service.

choices.text_html: Open it and check it yourself.
choices.feedback_html: Never attempt your own repair or bypass a fault. That is Biomedical Engineering's job.

choices.text_html: Biomedical Engineering.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. Biomedical Engineering runs the PPM programme and will inspect it.

choices.text_html: The supplier's sales representative.
choices.feedback_html: Inspection and PPM are coordinated by Biomedical Engineering. Report to them.

choices.text_html: IT support.
choices.feedback_html: IT handles network outages, not medical equipment. Notify Biomedical Engineering.

nodes.prompt_html: A colleague says: “Just take the pump from Room 5, nobody's using it.” What do you do?

choices.text_html: Don't move it yourself; ask Biomedical Engineering to arrange a replacement.
choices.feedback_html: Correct. Each location is assessed for the equipment placed there. Never relocate equipment without Biomedical Engineering, even temporarily.

choices.text_html: Move the pump from Room 5 — it's only for today.
choices.feedback_html: Even a temporary move bypasses the location assessment. Coordinate with Biomedical Engineering first.

feedback.correct_html: Spot it, report it: you stopped, tagged, notified Biomedical Engineering and did not relocate equipment.
feedback.incorrect_html: Review labels, tagging and the never-relocate rule, then try again.

screens.title: Oxygen cylinders
screens.prompt_html: True or false? Store oxygen cylinders upright and secured, with full and empty clearly separated.

feedback.correct_html: Correct — true. Secure them with a chain or stand, separate full from empty, and keep them away from flames, sparks and smoking.
feedback.incorrect_html: It is true. An unsecured cylinder can fall and be damaged, and mixing full with empty causes mistakes in an emergency.

screens.title: Ionising vs non-ionising
screens.prompt_html: Radiation is energy travelling as waves or particles.

tabs.label: Ionising
tabs.body_html: X-ray, CT. Enough energy to remove electrons from atoms: needs dosimeters, shielding and dose tracking.

tabs.label: Non-ionising
tabs.body_html: MRI, ultrasound, laser light. Lower energy, but still needs its own precautions.

tabs.label: MRI
tabs.body_html: The magnet is always on. No metal objects, oxygen cylinders or unscreened staff. Screening every time.

tabs.label: X-ray rooms
tabs.body_html: Wear a lead apron during exposure. Stand behind the shield or leave the room.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Ionising vs non-ionising. The MRI magnet is always on. Use the tabs as a short reference, not a checklist to race through. Notice which detail would guide your next conversation or decision. Use the principle in context. Keep the next action clear. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision. Notice which part of this you would use first on shift. The aim is a decision you can repeat, not a phrase to recall.

screens.title: Protection principles
screens.prompt_html: Match each radiation protection principle to its meaning.

pairs.right_html: The benefit must clearly justify the radiation risk.
Keep exposure as low as reasonably achievable (ALARA).
A firm upper dose limit applies to every worker and the public.

feedback.correct_html: Correct. Justify the exposure, optimise it, and never exceed the limit.
feedback.incorrect_html: Not quite. Justification asks “is it worth it?”, optimisation asks “is it as low as possible?”, limitation sets the ceiling.

screens.narration_text: Noor: The next choice asks you to apply the rule in a workplace situation. Read carefully, then choose.

screens.title: ALARA
screens.prompt_html: ALARA: As Low As Reasonably Achievable. Three levers you control.
screens.image_alt: ALARA: time, distance and shielding around a radiation source.

labels.text: Time — less time near the source, less dose
Distance — step back; intensity drops sharply
Shielding — aprons, barriers and walls absorb it

feedback.correct_html: Less time, more distance, the right shielding: three levers that lower your dose.
feedback.incorrect_html: Read each lever: time, distance and shielding all reduce exposure.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Time, distance, shielding — three levers you control. Use the labels to connect each part of the visual with the responsibility or action it supports. The diagram is a working reference, not a test to memorise. Think of the first detail you would check. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision.

screens.title: Staying accountable
screens.prompt_html: Staying accountable near radiation.

items.title: OSL dosimeter
items.body_html: Wear your Optically Stimulated Luminescence badge at all times in or near radiation areas.

items.title: Lead apron
items.body_html: Required whenever you are in the room during exposure, even for a quick scan.

items.title: RSO is your contact
items.body_html: The Radiation Safety Officer oversees compliance and dose records. Ask them about any radiation-safety concern.

screens.narration_text: Noor: Wear your badge. The RSO is your contact. Use each section to build the picture step by step. Before moving on, identify the action or check that belongs to your role. Apply the point to a familiar task. Carry the idea into your next decision. Notice which part of this you would use first on shift.

screens.title: Dose bands
screens.prompt_html: Your quarterly OSL reading shows 2.0 mSv. What happens? ⚠ Draft — pending 01/B4

options.text_html: Notification level: you are informed and placed under monitoring.

screens.title: Laser hazards and measures

blocks.html:
Hazards

  • Eyes — permanent damage, often with no pain at first
  • Skin — burns from direct or reflected beams
  • High voltage inside the equipment

screens.narration_text: Noor: Laser eye injuries often don't hurt at first — that's why protection is not optional. Keep the main point connected to a familiar task or conversation. That connection makes the information easier to use when it matters. The aim is a decision you can repeat, not a phrase to recall. Link it to the task waiting for you tomorrow.

screens.title: One shift, three plans
screens.intro_html:
{{asset:char-noor-avatar-neutral}}Noor · Safety liaison

One afternoon shift. Three things go wrong. Your decisions decide how it ends. No timer — take your time. You have 3 lives and one hint per situation.

hints.text: People first, then the hazard. Check the spill rule: volume and toxicity. ⚠ Draft — pending D1
Smoke means fire: Code Red. In RACE, rescue comes before extinguishing.
A label past its date means the device is not safe to use today.

nodes.content_html: 1 · 14:10. In a busy clinic, a cleaner knocks over a large 1-litre bottle of surface disinfectant. It spreads towards an oxygen cylinder. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Isolate the area, warn people, move the oxygen cylinder away and announce Code Orange.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Over the draft threshold, so Code Orange; and oxygen must be kept away from hazards. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Grab paper towels and mop it up yourself.
choices.feedback_html: A spill this size needs Code Orange, the right kit and PPE per the SDS. You lost a life. ⚠ Draft — pending D1

choices.text_html: Leave it to the cleaner and carry on with your patients.
choices.feedback_html: The hazard and the oxygen cylinder are still next to people. Isolate and warn first. You lost a life.

nodes.content_html: 2 · 15:30. The alarm sounds. Smoke is coming from the store room, and a patient is waiting in the chair beside the door.

choices.text_html: Code Red: move the patient away first, then raise the alarm and close the door.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Smoke means Code Red, and RACE starts with rescue.

choices.text_html: Code Orange: it could be the disinfectant from earlier.
choices.feedback_html: Smoke means fire: Code Red. The wrong code sends the wrong team. You lost a life.

choices.text_html: Go straight in with an extinguisher.
choices.feedback_html: The patient is still beside the smoke. Rescue comes before extinguishing. You lost a life.

nodes.content_html: 3 · 17:00. All clear. Dr. Omar needs suction for a patient and you notice the suction unit's inspection label has expired.

choices.text_html: Tag it “Out of Service”, use another approved unit, and notify Biomedical Engineering.
choices.feedback_html: Right. Dr. Omar: “That is the habit we want from every new colleague.”

choices.text_html: Use it — it switched on fine.
choices.feedback_html: Working is not the same as safe. Never use equipment past its due date. You lost a life.

choices.text_html: Fetch the unit from the next room without telling anyone.
choices.feedback_html: Never relocate equipment without Biomedical Engineering, and the expired unit is still untagged. You lost a life.

nodes.content_html:
Debrief: one shift, three plans

  • The spill — Hazmat & Waste plan (Code Orange), with Fire Safety (oxygen kept away).
  • The smoke — Fire Safety plan (Code Red, RACE) and Internal Disaster (code activation).
  • The suction unit — Biomedical plan (inspection label, out-of-service tag, Biomedical Engineering).

choices.text_html: Finish the shift and see your score.

feedback.correct_html: You connected three plans in one shift: people first, the right code, and equipment you can trust.
feedback.incorrect_html: Some decisions put people at risk. Review the debrief: Hazmat & Waste (spill), Fire Safety (RACE), Biomedical (labels). Then try again.

screens.notes: Companions: Noor, char-noor-explaining (host, intro) + Dr. Omar, char-omar-avatar-neutral in node 3 (his line is in the node feedback text; no companion is placed over the question). Speakers: Noor + Dr. Omar. Open decision D1: draft threshold ≥ 500 mL / highly toxic, reactive or explosive. Score counts best choices (1 point each, multiplier off); pass_score 2 of 3. Phase 3 rule “when wrong if lives==0 then goto debrief” is not expressible (GameAction has no goto); when lives run out the engine finalises the game as failed and shows the incorrect feedback, which carries the debrief summary. With 3 lives and 3 decision nodes, lives cannot reach 0 before the debrief.
